Analysis: Both hypotheses present innovative strategies to modify immunosuppressive cells in the tumor microenvironment, yet they differ in clarity and testability. Hypothesis 1, which targets mTOR signaling during EV uptake by neutrophils to block their conversion into immunosuppressive g-MDSCs, offers a more directly measurable and mechanistically coherent pathway. It leverages an established signaling cascade and has clear markers (e.g., phospho-mTOR and downstream effectors) that can be quantitatively assessed, rendering it highly testable. Although there are safety concerns due to the pleiotropic role of mTOR, these can be addressed with precise timing and targeted inhibition strategies. In contrast, Hypothesis 2 is appealing in its integration of the microbiota–MDSC–adenosine axis in colorectal cancer but suffers from less specific mechanistic detail and requires identification of exact microbial metabolites and signaling intermediates, making it more speculative and challenging to validate experimentally. Overall, Hypothesis 1 emerges as superior considering its novelty, greater plausibility, and higher testability despite needing refinements on safety aspects.
